narrative:
Your application for law school admission was rejected because the model predicts a 51% chance you'll fail the bar exam on your first try, just barely tipping over the edge into the "fail" category based on your profile. To understand why, consider "what if" scenarios called counterfactuals—these are alternative versions of your profile with minimal tweaks that would flip the model's prediction to a strong likelihood of passing the bar and getting your application approved. We generated three such scenarios, and in every single one, the only change needed was boosting your LSAT score from 34 to 36—a straightforward two-point increase. None of the counterfactuals touched your decile ranks, family income bracket, undergraduate GPA, or part-time status, signaling that the model sees your LSAT as the dominant hurdle right now, far outweighing those other factors in swaying the decision.

This pattern reveals that your LSAT is the linchpin: it changed 100% of the time across all scenarios, with an average bump of exactly 2 points, while everything else stayed fixed. Compared to typical accepted students, who often score in the upper 30s on the LSAT alongside stronger decile ranks, your current setup puts you on the bubble, but that small LSAT adjustment alone bridges the gap in the model's eyes.

The good news is this points to a realistic, targeted path forward—focus on prepping intensively for the LSAT to hit at least 36, perhaps through targeted practice tests or tutoring, since that's the minimal, proven shift that flips the prediction without overhauling your grades or background. Your solid undergraduate GPA already gives you an edge over many passers, so layering on that LSAT improvement could position you competitively. With part-time status being rare but viable for 7% of bar passers, sticking with it while nailing the LSAT keeps things feasible for your situation. Making this change could turn your 51% failure risk into a clear "pass" signal, opening the door to approval.
